sectionTitle: Waves in air, fluids and solids — part 4.6.1.5

specStatements.text: Students should be able to explain in qualitative terms, how the differences in velocity, absorption and reflection between different types of wave in solids and liquids can be used both for detection and exploration of structures which are hidden from direct observation.

Ultrasound waves have a frequency higher than the upper limit of hearing for humans. Ultrasound waves are partially reflected when they meet a boundary between two different media. The time taken for the reflections to reach a detector can be used to determine how far away such a boundary is. This allows ultrasound waves to be used for both medical and industrial imaging.

Seismic waves are produced by earthquakes. P-waves are longitudinal, seismic waves. P-waves travel at different speeds through solids and liquids. S-waves are transverse, seismic waves. S-waves cannot travel through a liquid. P-waves and S-waves provide evidence for the structure and size of the Earth’s core.
Echo sounding, using high frequency sound waves is used to detect objects in deep water and measure water depth.
Students should be aware that the study of seismic waves provided new evidence that led to discoveries about parts of the Earth which are not directly observable.

scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every explanation of detection and exploration is kept qualitative, exactly as the specification requires. Students are asked whether a wave speeds up, slows down, is reflected more or less strongly, or is absorbed more or less strongly — never to calculate a reflected fraction, an acoustic impedance, an attenuation coefficient or a refraction angle for a seismic or ultrasound wave. No quantitative absorption law is stated anywhere in this content.

scopeNotes.statement: The time taken for the reflections to reach a detector can be used to determine how far away such a boundary is.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: This section supplies no equation of its own, so no new equation is invented for it. Distance work uses only the specification's own relationship, distance travelled = speed × time, which students are required to recall elsewhere in this specification, together with the fact the specification itself states — that what is timed is a reflection, so the pulse has travelled to the boundary and back. Students are asked for the distance to the boundary, which is half the distance the pulse travels; they are never asked for anything beyond this.

scopeNotes.statement: P-waves and S-waves provide evidence for the structure and size of the Earth’s core.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The claim is kept as the specification makes it: the two wave types provide evidence about the structure and size of the core. Conclusions are drawn only from the two facts the specification gives — that S-waves cannot travel through a liquid, and that P-waves travel at different speeds through solids and liquids. Students are not required to name the boundaries or discontinuities inside the Earth, to state the depth or radius of the core, to give the physical reason why a liquid cannot carry a transverse wave, or to state a speed order for P-waves and S-waves, none of which this specification asks for.

concepts.definition: Sound waves with a frequency higher than the upper limit of hearing for humans. Ultrasound is ordinary sound — a longitudinal wave needing a medium to travel through — and differs from audible sound only in having too high a frequency for the human ear to detect.
The highest frequency a human ear can detect. This specification gives the normal range of human hearing as 20 Hz to 20 kHz, so any sound wave with a frequency above about 20 000 Hz is ultrasound.

The surface where one material meets a different material, such as the surface between two tissues in the body, between metal and the air inside a crack, or between water and the sea bed. A boundary matters because the wave behaves differently on each side of it — it travels at a different speed and is absorbed by a different amount.

When ultrasound waves meet a boundary between two different media they are partially reflected: part of the wave is reflected back towards the detector and the rest carries on into the second medium. Because the reflection is only partial, the transmitted part can go on to reflect from deeper boundaries, so several boundaries can be found from a single pulse.

concepts.term: Finding a distance from the time of a reflection
concepts.definition: The time taken for a reflection to reach a detector is used to work out how far away the boundary is. The distance the pulse travels is found from distance travelled = speed × time, using the speed of the wave in that medium. Because the pulse travels to the boundary and back, the distance to the boundary is half the distance the pulse has travelled.

A use of ultrasound in which a pulse is sent into the body and the reflections from the boundaries between different tissues are timed. Each boundary returns its reflection after a different time, so the depths of the boundaries can be found and built into an image of a structure that cannot be seen directly.

A use of ultrasound in which a pulse is sent into a manufactured object, such as a metal casting or a weld. A crack or void inside the object is a boundary between two different media, so it partially reflects the pulse; a reflection arriving earlier than the reflection from the far side shows that a flaw lies inside the object.

The transfer of energy from a wave to the material it is passing through, which reduces the energy the wave carries. Different types of wave are absorbed by different amounts in the same material, so a wave that is only weakly absorbed by a material can be used to explore what lies beyond it, while a strongly absorbed wave cannot.

concepts.term: Velocity of a wave in a medium
concepts.definition: The speed at which a wave travels through a particular material. The same wave travels at different speeds in different solids and liquids, and different types of wave travel at different speeds through the same material. A change of speed at a boundary is what makes the boundary reflect part of the wave, and the speed must be known before a time can be turned into a distance.
Waves produced by earthquakes, which travel through the Earth and are picked up by detectors at the surface. They are of two kinds, P-waves and S-waves.
A longitudinal seismic wave. P-waves travel at different speeds through solids and liquids, so their speed changes when they cross from one part of the Earth's interior into another.
A transverse seismic wave. S-waves cannot travel through a liquid, so any region of the Earth's interior that S-waves fail to cross is evidence that the material there is liquid.

P-waves and S-waves provide evidence for the structure and size of the Earth's core. Detectors on the far side of the Earth from an earthquake receive no S-waves, which is evidence that part of the core is liquid; P-waves do arrive, but their speed changes where they cross into and out of the core, which alters the paths they follow and gives evidence about the size of the core and the structure within it.

The use of high frequency sound waves to detect objects in deep water and to measure water depth. A pulse is sent down from a ship, and the time for the echo to return from the sea bed or from an object is used to find how far away it is.

Structures that cannot be seen or reached — the inside of a body, a flaw inside a solid casting, the sea bed under deep water, the interior of the Earth. Waves reach these structures and return, so their differences in velocity, absorption and reflection allow the structures to be detected and explored indirectly. The study of seismic waves provided new evidence of exactly this kind, leading to discoveries about parts of the Earth which are not directly observable.

concepts.term: Detection and exploration using differences between waves
concepts.definition: Detection means finding that something is there; exploration means working out its size, depth or structure. Both rest on the same three differences: a wave travelling at a different velocity in the hidden material is partially reflected at its boundary, the time of that reflection gives the distance, and a wave that is weakly absorbed by the material in between is the one that can reach the structure and return.

misconceptions.question: Does a wave travel at the same speed in every material?
misconceptions.correct: No. The speed of a wave depends on the material it is travelling through, and it changes when the wave crosses into a different material.
misconceptions.misconception: A wave has one speed of its own, so it travels just as fast through rock, water or metal as it does through air.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn a single quoted value for the speed of sound (about 330 m/s) or the speed of light early on and treat it as a property of the wave rather than of the wave in a particular medium. Speeds in solids and liquids are rarely quoted alongside it.
misconceptions.correction: Velocity is one of the three differences the specification names. It is precisely because a wave travels at a different speed in the hidden material that a boundary reflects part of the wave and can be detected. It also means the correct speed for that medium must be used when a time is turned into a distance.

misconceptions.question: When a wave meets a boundary, is it all reflected or all transmitted?
misconceptions.correct: Neither. Part of the wave is reflected back and the rest carries on into the second medium — the reflection is partial.
misconceptions.misconception: A wave either bounces off a boundary completely, like a ball off a wall, or goes straight through it as if the boundary were not there.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Reflection is first met with light and plane mirrors, where almost all of the light comes back, and transmission is first met with clear glass, where almost all of it goes through. Students carry over an all-or-nothing picture.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states that ultrasound waves are partially reflected at a boundary between two different media. This is essential: if the first boundary reflected everything, nothing could be learned about anything deeper, and imaging would be impossible.

misconceptions.question: If a material absorbs a wave strongly, does a strong signal come back?
misconceptions.correct: No. Absorption transfers the wave's energy to the material, so less energy carries on and less returns to the detector.
misconceptions.misconception: Absorbed and reflected mean much the same thing — the material takes the wave in and sends it back.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The everyday word 'absorb' suggests soaking something up and holding it, and students meet 'absorbed' and 'reflected' in the same list of things that happen at a surface, so the two get blurred.
misconceptions.correction: Absorption and reflection are different and are named separately by the specification. A strongly absorbing layer weakens or removes reflections from everything beneath it, which is why the wave chosen for a survey must be one that the material in between absorbs only weakly.

misconceptions.question: Does a wave change frequency when it enters a different material?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is the velocity of the wave that differs from material to material; the frequency is set by the source.
misconceptions.misconception: The hidden layer is found because the wave comes back with a different frequency from the one that was sent in.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know something must change at a boundary, and frequency is the wave property they can name most readily. Everyday talk about signals 'changing frequency' reinforces it.
misconceptions.correction: The three differences the specification names are velocity, absorption and reflection. Detection depends on the change of velocity at the boundary, the partial reflection this produces, and the time that reflection takes to return — not on any change of frequency.

misconceptions.question: Is ultrasound a kind of radiation, like X-rays?
misconceptions.correct: No. Ultrasound is sound — a mechanical wave that needs a medium — and it is not part of the electromagnetic spectrum.
misconceptions.misconception: Ultrasound must be a type of radiation, because it is used in hospital scanners in the same way X-rays are.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both are met as 'scans' in a medical context, and both are described as passing into the body. The prefix 'ultra' also echoes 'ultraviolet', which is electromagnetic.
misconceptions.correction: Ultrasound waves are sound waves with a frequency higher than the upper limit of hearing for humans. An ultrasound image is built from reflections timed at a detector, not from radiation passing through the body onto a film.

misconceptions.question: Does 'ultrasound' mean sound that is extremely loud?
misconceptions.correct: No. It means sound of a frequency above the upper limit of human hearing. Loudness is not what makes it ultrasound.
misconceptions.misconception: Ultrasound is sound too powerful for the ear to cope with, so you cannot hear it because it would deafen you.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday use of 'ultra' means extreme, and students routinely confuse frequency (pitch) with amplitude (loudness), which are separate wave properties.
misconceptions.correction: The definition is about frequency alone. A quiet ultrasound wave is still ultrasound; a very loud 500 Hz note is not, because 500 Hz is within the range of human hearing.

misconceptions.question: If an echo returns after 0.8 s, do I multiply speed by 0.8 s to get the depth?
misconceptions.correct: That gives the total distance the pulse travelled. The pulse went down and came back, so the depth is half of it.
misconceptions.misconception: The time measured is the time for the pulse to reach the boundary, so speed × time gives the distance to the boundary.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students apply distance = speed × time correctly but do not picture the path. The time is the one quantity given in the question, so it is used without asking what journey it belongs to.
misconceptions.correction: What is timed is a reflection, so the time covers the journey to the boundary and the journey back. Work out speed × time first, then halve it to get the distance to the boundary. Halving is the step examiners look for.

misconceptions.question: Ultrasound is outside the range of human hearing — is it above or below it?
misconceptions.correct: Above. Ultrasound waves have a frequency higher than the upper limit of hearing for humans.
misconceptions.misconception: Ultrasound is sound that is too low for people to hear, below the bottom of the hearing range.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember only that ultrasound is 'outside what we can hear' and then guess the wrong end of the range, or confuse it with infrasound, which is genuinely below the lower limit.
misconceptions.correction: The specification is explicit: higher than the upper limit of hearing. With the range of human hearing given as 20 Hz to 20 kHz, ultrasound is above 20 kHz.

misconceptions.question: Which seismic wave is longitudinal and which is transverse?
misconceptions.correct: P-waves are longitudinal, seismic waves. S-waves are transverse, seismic waves.
misconceptions.misconception: P-waves are transverse and S-waves are longitudinal.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two labels are arbitrary letters with nothing in them to cue the answer, so a student with no memory hook has an even chance of swapping them. The swap then corrupts every conclusion drawn afterwards.
misconceptions.correction: Fix the pairing first: P for longitudinal (a push wave, like sound), S for transverse (a shake wave, side to side). The rest of the topic depends on it, because it is the transverse S-wave that cannot travel through a liquid.

misconceptions.question: Can any seismic wave travel through a liquid?
misconceptions.correct: P-waves can travel through liquids as well as solids, though at a different speed. S-waves cannot travel through a liquid.
misconceptions.misconception: A liquid stops seismic waves, so neither P-waves nor S-waves get through it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember 'liquid blocks seismic waves' as a single simplified rule instead of the distinction the specification draws between the two wave types.
misconceptions.correction: The contrast between the two is the whole point. If liquid stopped both, no wave would arrive from the far side of the Earth and there would be nothing to compare. It is because P-waves arrive and S-waves do not that a liquid region can be identified.

misconceptions.question: Do P-waves travel at one steady speed all the way through the Earth?
misconceptions.correct: No. P-waves travel at different speeds through solids and liquids, so their speed changes as they pass through different regions.
misconceptions.misconception: P-waves have a fixed speed, so their arrival times tell you only how far away the earthquake was.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Speed is usually treated as a single given number in calculations, and a picture of the Earth's interior as uniform makes a changing speed seem unnecessary.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states directly that P-waves travel at different speeds through solids and liquids. These speed changes at boundaries alter the paths the waves follow, and that is a large part of the evidence for the size and structure of the core.

misconceptions.question: S-waves do not reach the far side of the Earth. Does that mean the core is empty?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is evidence that part of the core is liquid — a liquid cannot carry S-waves, but it is still material.
misconceptions.misconception: The missing S-waves show there is a hollow space or gap inside the Earth for them to fall into.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know a wave that fails to arrive has been blocked, and the most vivid picture of 'nothing there' is a hole. The role of P-waves, which do arrive, is overlooked.
misconceptions.correction: P-waves cross the core and are detected, so the core is certainly not empty. The specific fact that S-waves cannot travel through a liquid is what makes their absence evidence for a liquid region.

misconceptions.question: As a seismic wave passes through rock, does the rock travel with it?
misconceptions.correct: No. The rock oscillates about its position; the wave transfers energy through the rock without transferring the rock itself.
misconceptions.misconception: The wave carries the rock along with it, which is why the ground moves in an earthquake.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Earthquake footage shows the ground visibly moving and objects being carried, and students transfer the idea of a moving substance to the wave itself.
misconceptions.correction: In a P-wave the rock oscillates back and forth parallel to the direction the wave travels; in an S-wave it oscillates at right angles to that direction. In both, the material returns to where it started and only energy is transferred onwards.

misconceptions.question: Why not use light or radio waves instead of sound to find the depth of the sea?
misconceptions.correct: Water absorbs light and radio waves very strongly, so they do not travel far enough through deep water to return a usable reflection.
misconceptions.misconception: Any wave would do the job; sound is used out of habit, and light or radar would work just as well underwater.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Radar and light-based rangefinders are familiar from the air, and students do not meet the fact that water is a strong absorber of both.
misconceptions.correction: This is exactly the use of the differences in absorption that the specification refers to. High frequency sound travels well through water and reflects from the sea bed and from objects in it, so echo sounding uses sound.

misconceptions.question: Does sound travel faster than light through water?
misconceptions.correct: No. Light travels far faster than sound in water; sound is used because it is absorbed much less, not because it is faster.
misconceptions.misconception: Sound is used underwater because sound goes faster in water than light does.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn that sound travels faster in water than in air and turn this into a general claim that sound is fast in water. Speed is also the reason they are readiest to reach for.
misconceptions.correction: Speed is not the reason. The reason echo sounding uses high frequency sound is that water absorbs sound weakly and absorbs light and radio waves strongly, so only the sound pulse returns from the sea bed.

misconceptions.question: How do we know what the inside of the Earth is like — has anyone been there?
misconceptions.correct: No one has. The evidence comes from studying seismic waves that have travelled through the Earth and been detected at the surface.
misconceptions.misconception: Scientists have drilled down and brought up samples of the core, and the seismic wave evidence just backs that up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Samples of rock and drilling are familiar from geology lessons, and diagrams of the Earth's layers are drawn with such confidence that they look like something someone has seen.
misconceptions.correction: The core has never been reached or sampled. The specification's point is precisely that the study of seismic waves provided new evidence which led to discoveries about parts of the Earth which are not directly observable.

misconceptions.question: If nobody can observe the core, is what we say about it just a guess?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is a conclusion drawn from measurements of real waves that have passed through the Earth — indirect evidence, not guesswork.
misconceptions.misconception: Anything you cannot see for yourself cannot really be known, so the liquid core is just a theory somebody made up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students equate evidence with seeing, and the everyday use of 'theory' to mean 'hunch' encourages them to treat an indirectly supported conclusion as unsupported.
misconceptions.correction: Indirect evidence is still evidence. Detectors record which waves arrive, when, and from which directions; those measurements can only be explained by particular structures inside the Earth. This is how discoveries were made about parts of the Earth that are not directly observable.

mcqs.stem: Waves are sent down into the ground to search for a hidden layer of rock, in which the waves would travel at a different speed. What happens where the waves reach the top of the hidden layer?

options.text: The wave carries on at exactly the same speed as before
options.rationale: A student who treats speed as a fixed property of the wave rather than of the medium sees no reason for anything to change at the boundary.

options.text: The whole wave is reflected and none carries on downwards
options.rationale: The all-or-nothing picture of reflection learned from mirrors. It also implies nothing below the layer could ever be surveyed.

options.text: Part of the wave is reflected and part carries on downwards
options.rationale: A change of velocity at a boundary between two different media produces a partial reflection. The reflected part returns to the detector and reveals the layer; the transmitted part continues and can reflect from deeper boundaries.

options.text: The wave carries on but with a higher frequency than before
options.rationale: Students know something must change at a boundary and reach for frequency, the wave property they can name most easily.

mcqs.stem: In a survey, the waves pass easily through layer X but are strongly absorbed by layer Y, which lies beneath it. What effect does this have on the survey?

options.text: A strong reflection returns from layer Y because it absorbs waves
options.rationale: Chosen by students who treat 'absorbed' and 'reflected' as describing the same event at a surface.

options.text: No reflections at all are received, even from the top of layer Y
options.rationale: The all-or-nothing view again: the layer is imagined as stopping everything, ignoring the partial reflection from its own upper boundary.

options.text: Waves below layer Y speed up to make up for the energy they lost
options.rationale: A conflation of energy with speed; students assume a wave that has lost energy compensates by travelling faster.

options.text: Reflections from below layer Y are weak or missing at the detector
options.rationale: Absorption transfers the wave's energy to layer Y, so little energy reaches anything below it and little returns. A strongly absorbing layer hides whatever lies beneath it.

mcqs.stem: Differences in which three properties, between different types of wave in solids and liquids, are used to detect and explore hidden structures?

options.text: Velocity, absorption and reflection
options.rationale: These are the three properties named in the specification, and each has a distinct role: velocity change creates the reflection, reflection returns the signal, and low absorption lets the wave reach the structure and come back.

options.text: Frequency, absorption and reflection
options.rationale: Picked by students who believe the useful change at a boundary is a change of frequency.

options.text: Amplitude, absorption and reflection
options.rationale: A student who thinks a wave has one fixed speed everywhere sees no way velocity could be useful and substitutes amplitude.

options.text: Velocity, absorption and refraction
options.rationale: Reflection and refraction are easily swapped, and refraction is the more technical-sounding word of the two.

mcqs.stem: Which statement correctly describes ultrasound waves?

options.text: Sound waves with a frequency above the upper limit of human hearing
options.rationale: This is the specification's definition. Ultrasound is sound; only its frequency puts it beyond what the ear can detect.

options.text: Sound waves that are much louder than a human ear can safely hear
options.rationale: Chosen by students who read 'ultra' as extreme and confuse frequency with loudness.

options.text: Electromagnetic waves used to make images of the inside of the body
options.rationale: Medical scanning is associated with X-rays, so ultrasound gets classed as radiation rather than sound.

options.text: Sound waves with a frequency below the lower limit of human hearing
options.rationale: Students who remember only that ultrasound lies outside the hearing range pick the wrong end of it.

mcqs.stem: An ultrasound pulse sent into the body meets three tissue boundaries one after another. Why can a reflection be received from all three?

options.text: The pulse is reflected in full at each boundary that it reaches
options.rationale: Total reflection at the first boundary would leave nothing to reach the second, but students holding the all-or-nothing view do not notice the contradiction.

options.text: Only part of the pulse reflects at each boundary; the rest goes on
options.rationale: Ultrasound is partially reflected at a boundary between two different media, so the transmitted part survives to reach and reflect from the next boundary.

options.text: The pulse speeds up at each boundary, so it reaches them all
options.rationale: Speed is offered as the explanation by students who have not connected reaching a boundary with being partially transmitted.

options.text: The pulse is absorbed at each boundary and then sent out again
options.rationale: Absorption is imagined as taking the wave in and releasing it again, which blurs it with reflection.

mcqs.stem: An ultrasound pulse is sent into a steel block to look for a crack. Ultrasound travels at 6000 m/s in the steel. A reflection from the crack is received 0.000 040 s after the pulse is sent. How far below the surface is the crack?

options.rationale: The full there-and-back distance, taken as the depth because the pulse's return journey was not accounted for.
Obtained by using 330 m/s, the speed of sound in air, instead of the speed in steel, by a student who treats speed as fixed for the wave.
The result of halving twice — once by using half the time and again at the end — a common double-correction error.
distance travelled = speed × time = 6000 × 0.000 040 = 0.24 m. The pulse travelled to the crack and back, so the crack is 0.24 ÷ 2 = 0.12 m below the surface.

mcqs.stem: A pulse of ultrasound is sent into a steel casting. From one region a reflection returns much sooner than the reflection from the far side of the casting. What is the best conclusion?

options.text: A boundary such as a crack lies inside that region
options.rationale: An earlier reflection means a shorter distance travelled, so there is a boundary between two different media nearer the surface than the far side — a flaw inside the casting.

options.text: The casting must be thicker in that region than elsewhere
options.rationale: The time-distance relationship is inverted: a student reasons that a bigger reading of any kind means more metal.

options.text: The ultrasound was completely absorbed in that region
options.rationale: Absorption is offered as the cause of a returning signal, which only makes sense if absorption and reflection are treated as the same thing.

options.text: The ultrasound was completely reflected at the outer surface
options.rationale: Total reflection at the surface would give the same early return everywhere, not from one region only, but the all-or-nothing view makes it attractive.

mcqs.stem: Which statement explains how an ultrasound scan builds up an image of a structure inside the body?

options.text: Ultrasound is absorbed by bone, casting a shadow onto a film
options.rationale: This describes an X-ray radiograph and is picked by students who treat ultrasound as a form of radiation.

options.text: Ultrasound is completely reflected by the first tissue it meets
options.rationale: The all-or-nothing view of reflection, which would in fact make imaging of anything deeper impossible.

options.text: Reflections from boundaries between tissues arrive at different times
options.rationale: Each boundary partially reflects the pulse, and the time each reflection takes to reach the detector gives the distance to that boundary, so the depths can be assembled into an image.

options.text: Ultrasound is absorbed by the tissues and then re-emitted by them
options.rationale: Absorption is imagined as storing and re-releasing the wave, blurring it with reflection.

mcqs.stem: Which statement correctly describes P-waves and S-waves?

options.text: P-waves are transverse and S-waves are longitudinal
options.rationale: The straight swap. The letters carry no clue to the answer, so a student without a memory hook picks either way.

options.text: P-waves are longitudinal and S-waves are transverse
options.rationale: Exactly as the specification states: P-waves are longitudinal, seismic waves and S-waves are transverse, seismic waves.

options.text: Both are longitudinal, like all waves in solid rock
options.rationale: Chosen by students who generalise from sound, the longitudinal wave they know, to all waves in a solid.

options.text: Both carry the rock along with them as they travel
options.rationale: Attractive to students who picture earthquake damage and think the wave transports material rather than energy.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about seismic waves travelling through the Earth is correct?

options.text: Neither S-waves nor P-waves can travel through any liquid
options.rationale: The over-simplified rule 'liquid stops seismic waves', which loses the contrast the evidence depends on.

options.text: S-waves can travel through any liquid, but P-waves cannot
options.rationale: The consequence of having the two wave types the wrong way round.

options.text: S-waves cannot travel through a liquid, but P-waves can
options.rationale: The specification states that S-waves cannot travel through a liquid; P-waves do travel through liquids, though at a different speed from in solids.

options.text: P-waves travel at one fixed speed through solid and liquid
options.rationale: Chosen by students who treat wave speed as a single fixed number regardless of the medium.

mcqs.stem: After an earthquake, detectors on the far side of the Earth receive P-waves but no S-waves. What does this provide evidence for?

options.text: The core is a hollow space with no material inside it at all
options.rationale: 'Blocked' is read as 'nothing there', and the arrival of the P-waves is overlooked.

options.text: S-waves are transverse, so they cannot travel through a solid
options.rationale: A garbled version of the rule, applied to solids instead of liquids, which would mean S-waves could never be detected at all.

options.text: Part of the core is liquid, so S-waves cannot pass through it
options.rationale: S-waves cannot travel through a liquid, so their failure to arrive is evidence of a liquid region; the P-waves that do arrive show there is material there to travel through.

options.text: The core is solid, and it absorbed the S-waves completely
options.rationale: Absorption is offered in place of the specific fact about liquids, by students who use it as a general explanation for any missing wave.

mcqs.stem: How do P-waves provide evidence about the size of the Earth's core?

options.text: Their speed changes at the core boundary, bending their paths
options.rationale: P-waves travel at different speeds through solids and liquids, so their speed changes where they enter and leave the core; the resulting paths and arrival points give evidence about how large the core is.

options.text: They cannot enter the core, so a total shadow is produced
options.rationale: The rule about S-waves and liquids is transferred to P-waves, which do in fact cross the core.

options.text: They travel at one steady speed everywhere inside the Earth
options.rationale: A uniform-Earth picture, which would leave nothing for the arrival times to reveal about structure.

options.text: They become transverse waves once inside the liquid core
options.rationale: Chosen by students who are unsure which wave type is which and think the type can change en route.

mcqs.stem: A P-wave travels through solid rock. How does the rock move as the wave passes?

options.text: At right angles to the direction the wave travels
options.rationale: This describes a transverse wave and is chosen when P and S are the wrong way round.

options.text: The rock itself is carried along with the wave
options.rationale: The wave is pictured as transporting material rather than transferring energy through it.

options.text: Parallel to the direction in which the wave travels
options.rationale: P-waves are longitudinal, so the oscillations of the rock are parallel to the direction of energy transfer.

options.text: In circles around a point on the wave's path
options.rationale: Borrowed from pictures of floating objects on water waves, which students generalise to waves in solids.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about echo sounding is correct?

options.text: Radio pulses are used because they travel well through water
options.rationale: Radar is familiar from use in air, and students do not know that water absorbs radio waves strongly.

options.text: High frequency sound is used to find depth and locate objects
options.rationale: Echo sounding, using high frequency sound waves, is used to detect objects in deep water and to measure water depth.

options.text: Light pulses are used because light travels fastest in water
options.rationale: Speed is reached for as the deciding factor, when the deciding factor is in fact absorption.

options.text: Sound is used, but only the outward trip of the pulse is timed
options.rationale: The there-and-back path is not pictured, so the measured time is taken to be a one-way time.

mcqs.stem: A ship uses echo sounding to measure the depth of the sea. The speed of the sound waves in the sea water is 1500 m/s and the echo from the sea bed returns 0.80 s after the pulse is sent out. How deep is the water?

options.rationale: The total distance the pulse travelled, used as the depth because the return journey was not allowed for.
Obtained by using 330 m/s, the speed of sound in air, by a student who treats the speed of sound as one fixed value.
The result of dividing 1500 by 0.80 instead of multiplying — a very common slip when the time is less than one second.
distance travelled = speed × time = 1500 × 0.80 = 1200 m. That is down and back, so the depth is 1200 ÷ 2 = 600 m.

mcqs.stem: Echo sounding uses high frequency sound waves rather than light or radio waves. Why?

options.text: Light and radio pulses would work just as well at any depth
options.rationale: Chosen by students who assume any wave can be used and that sound is simply traditional.

options.text: Sound travels faster through sea water than light does
options.rationale: Speed is offered instead of absorption, and 'sound travels faster in water' is over-generalised.

options.text: Sound waves are the only waves that reflect off a sea bed
options.rationale: Reflection is treated as belonging to sound alone, which ignores that all waves can be reflected at a boundary.

options.text: Water absorbs light and radio waves much more strongly than sound
options.rationale: This is a difference in absorption between types of wave. Only the sound pulse travels far enough through deep water and returns strongly enough to be detected.

mcqs.stem: Why was the study of seismic waves so important for our knowledge of the Earth?

options.text: It confirmed what had already been seen by drilling to the core
options.rationale: Students assume the layers in textbook diagrams must have been sampled at some point.

options.text: It proved that the inside of the Earth cannot be studied at all
options.rationale: Picked by students who equate evidence with seeing and conclude the interior is unknowable.

options.text: It allows the exact time of the next earthquake to be predicted
options.rationale: Prediction is the use of earthquake science students expect, and it is easily confused with what the waves actually reveal.

options.text: It gave new evidence about regions nobody can observe directly
options.rationale: The study of seismic waves provided new evidence that led to discoveries about parts of the Earth which are not directly observable.

mcqs.stem: Measurements of seismic waves led scientists to conclude that part of the Earth's core is liquid. This conclusion is an example of scientists:

options.text: taking samples of the core from very deep mines and boreholes
options.rationale: Chosen by students who assume knowledge of the interior must have come from physical samples.

options.text: using indirect evidence to reach a conclusion about a hidden region
options.rationale: The waves themselves are measured at the surface; the structure they passed through is inferred from which waves arrive and when. That is indirect evidence, and it is how parts of the Earth that are not directly observable came to be known.

options.text: guessing, because a hidden region cannot be studied by evidence
options.rationale: Reflects the belief that a conclusion not based on seeing something is merely an opinion.

options.text: confirming an idea by observing the core region of the Earth directly
options.rationale: Confident textbook diagrams of the interior make direct observation sound as though it must have happened.
